scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Yangju byeolsandae nori was started by government officials working in Yangju province after a group of entertainers called Ttakttakyipae from Hanyang frequently broke their promise to perform.
Lee Eul-chuk was the main organiser and first to produce mask dramas in Yangju, leveraging the town's status as a transport hub and administrative center.

Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed primarily in April, May, July, and August, as well as during rain-praying ceremonies.
It begins with a ritual ceremony praying for a good performance where traditional foods like jora, tteok, colored fruits, a beef head, and a pork leg are served.
Costs were traditionally covered by rich locals and merchants, while performers were unpaid.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The performance is organized primarily around dancing, miming, and drama with actors executing set lines in prose.
The dance style is divided into geodeureumsik and kkaekkisik.
Some character roles rely entirely on dancing and gestures without spoken words, while others combine dialogue with movement.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The main instruments used in the performance are two piri flutes, one jeotdae, one haegeum, one janggu drum, and one buk drum.
A kkwaenggari gong is added when needed, and performances occasionally rely solely on the piri and janggu.
Listen for the two piri, one jeotdae, one haegeum, one janggu.

Played with traditional Korean instruments including two piri flutes, a jeotdae, a haegeum, a janggu drum, and a buk drum, occasionally supplemented by a kkwaenggari gong and driven by taryong or gutgurigok rhythms.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performances took place at Sagikgol, north of Mount Bulgok, near a shaman house where props were stored.
The production features thirty-two traditional characters, but because some masks are utilized in multiple roles, only twenty-two masks are worn during the performance.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Lee Eul-chuk is recorded as the main organiser of the show and the first to produce mask dramas in Yangju.

The tradition spread mainly from Seoul and Gyeonggi Province to Aeohgae, Manrijae, Gameundol, Nokbeon, Sajikgol, Gupabal, Nodes, Toegyewon and Uijeongbu, though it is no longer performed in these external regions.
Originated from sandae gabhee, a welcoming ceremony for Chinese diplomats, and is also called sandi nori, sanji nori, or sandu nori.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Yangju byeolsandae nori is parent of sandae gabhee: Welcoming ceremony for Chinese diplomats from which sandae nori originally descended.
Yangju byeolsandae nori is sibling of Bongsan Talchum: Another prominent Korean mask dance tradition, contrasted by Bongsan's verse lines versus Yangju's prose lines.
